title: Excel and productivity
desc: Formulas, shortcuts and clean-data habits for everyday sales admin

pages.t: A sheet is a grid of cells. Each has an address like B2 (column B, row 2). A group of cells is a range, written B2:B10. Type = first and Excel treats what follows as a formula, such as =B2*C2.
g: Range
A block of cells, written first cell:last cell, like B2:B10.
Formula
A cell entry that starts with = and calculates a result.

pages.h: What you see is not what is stored
pages.t: A cell can show 12% while holding 0.12, or show a date while holding a number. Formatting changes only the look. The value underneath is what formulas use. Clicking a cell shows its real content in the formula bar above the grid.
g: Formula bar
The bar above the grid showing what a cell really contains.

pages.t: Select a price list and choose Home, Format as Table. You get a header row with filter buttons on every column, and a formula typed in one cell is applied down the whole column. Formulas can then use column names instead of cell addresses.
g: Table
An Excel feature that turns a range into one managed unit with headers and filters.

quiz.q: A cell shows 12% but a formula treats it as 0.12. Why?
o: Formatting changes how a value looks, not the stored value
Excel always divides percentages by ten
quiz.w: Formatting is only the look. The value underneath is what formulas use, and the formula bar shows it.

quiz.q: What does the range B2:B10 mean?
o: The cells from B2 down to B10 in column B
Row 2 to row 10 in every column
quiz.w: A range is written first cell, colon, last cell. B2:B10 is the block of cells in column B from row 2 to row 10.

quiz.q: You format a price list as a table. What do you get on every column?
o: A header row with filter buttons
An automatic total at the bottom of the screen
quiz.w: A table has a header row by default, with filter and sort controls on each column.

src.l: Microsoft: Switch between relative, absolute and mixed references

pages.t: Write =B4*C4 in D4 (price times quantity) and copy it to D5. Excel gives =B5*C5. That is a relative reference: it moves with the formula. This is usually what you want when copying a formula down a list.
g: Relative reference
A reference like B4 that shifts when the formula is copied.

pages.t: Say a discount sits in cell F1 and every row must use it. Write $F$1. The dollar signs lock column and row, so the reference stays put when copied. This is an absolute reference. $F1 locks only the column, F$1 only the row.
g: Absolute reference
A reference like $F$1 that does not change when copied.
Mixed reference
Locks only the column ($F1) or only the row (F$1).

pages.h: F4 types the dollars for you
pages.t: On Windows, click into a formula, select the reference with the cursor and press F4. Each press cycles through the reference types, so you do not type the dollar signs by hand. If copied formulas give odd results down a list, a missing dollar sign is the first suspect.

quiz.q: You copy =B4*C4 from D4 to D5. What does D5 contain?
quiz.w: Relative references shift with the formula, so row 4 becomes row 5.

quiz.q: A discount in F1 must apply to every row. Which reference do you use for it?
quiz.w: $F$1 locks both column and row, so every copy still points at F1.

quiz.q: Which key cycles a reference between relative, absolute and mixed?
quiz.w: Select the reference in the formula and press F4 to cycle the types.

quiz.q: Copied formulas down a list give odd results. What do you check first?
o: A missing dollar sign on a fixed cell
quiz.w: A reference that should be locked but is not will drift when the formula is copied.

pages.t: =SUM(B2:B10) adds the numbers, and it ignores text. =AVERAGE(B2:B10) gives the mean: text and empty cells are ignored, but zeros are included. On Windows, Alt+= inserts a SUM for you.
g: AVERAGE
The arithmetic mean of the numbers in a range.

pages.t: =COUNT(B2:B10) counts only cells holding numbers. =COUNTA(A2:A10) counts every non-empty cell, including text. Use COUNTA to find out how many customers are on a list, and COUNT to count how many have an order value.
g: COUNTA
Counts all cells that are not empty.

pages.t: =IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false) returns one of two results. For example =IF(C2>=10,"In stock","Check") labels a stock list row by row. Text in a formula goes inside double quotes.
g: Logical test
A comparison like C2>=10 that is either true or false.

quiz.q: A list of 50 customer names is in A2:A51. Which formula counts them?
quiz.w: COUNTA counts non-empty cells including text. COUNT only counts numbers, so it would return 0 for names.

quiz.q: How does AVERAGE treat a cell containing 0?
quiz.w: Cells with the value zero are included. Empty cells and text are ignored.

quiz.q: Which formula labels stock of 10 or more as In stock?
quiz.w: IF takes the test first, then the result if true, then the result if false.

src.l: Microsoft: Detect formula errors in Excel

pages.t: Excel errors start with # and tell you what went wrong. #DIV/0! means dividing by zero or an empty cell. #NAME? means Excel does not recognise text in the formula, often a misspelt function. #### usually means the column is too narrow.

#N/A: a value is not available, typically a lookup found no match. #REF!: a referenced cell was deleted or pasted over, and Undo can help. #VALUE!: the formula mixes data types, for example doing maths on text.

=IFERROR(value, value_if_error) replaces an error with a result you choose, such as =IFERROR(A2/B2,0). It catches every error type, even real mistakes, so use it only when you are sure the formula works as intended.
g: IFERROR
A wrapper that shows your own result instead of any formula error.

quiz.q: A lookup shows #N/A. What does that most likely mean?
quiz.w: #N/A means a value is not available to the formula. For lookups it usually means there is no match.

quiz.q: You see #### in a cell. What is the usual cause?
o: The column is too narrow to show the content
quiz.w: #### means the column is too narrow (or a negative date). Widening the column fixes it.

quiz.q: Why should you be careful with IFERROR?
o: It hides every kind of error, including real mistakes
quiz.w: IFERROR covers all error types, so a genuine problem can be masked.

pages.h: Lookups fetch a value by key
pages.t: You have an order list with item numbers and a stock list with names. A lookup finds each item number in the stock list and brings back the name. It is among the most useful formulas in sales admin and saves hours of copy and paste.
g: Lookup
A formula that finds a key in one list and returns related data from the same row.

pages.t: =VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, FALSE). You count columns by hand, and the key must sit in the leftmost column, with the answer to its right. Leave out the last argument and it defaults to approximate match, which can return wrong results.
g: Approximate match
Finds the closest value and assumes a sorted list. Use FALSE for an exact match.

pages.t: =XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found]). It defaults to exact match, can look to the left, and lets you write your own not-found text. It is in Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and 2024, but not Excel 2016 or 2019.

quiz.q: What is a VLOOKUP restriction?
o: The key must be in the leftmost column of the range
quiz.w: VLOOKUP searches the first column of the table array and returns from columns to its right.

quiz.q: You omit the last VLOOKUP argument. What happens?
quiz.w: The default is approximate match, which assumes a sorted first column. Use FALSE for exact.

quiz.q: A colleague has Excel 2019 and opens your sheet with XLOOKUP. What is the issue?
o: XLOOKUP is not available in Excel 2016 or 2019
quiz.w: XLOOKUP is available in Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and 2024, but not in Excel 2016 or 2019.

quiz.q: Which feature does XLOOKUP have that VLOOKUP lacks?
quiz.w: XLOOKUP has an if_not_found argument, and it uses separate lookup and return ranges instead of a column number.

pages.t: SUMIF adds values that meet one condition: =SUMIF(B2:B5,"John",C2:C5) totals column C where column B says John. The order is range to test, condition, then range to add.
g: Criteria
The condition a cell must meet to be counted or added.

pages.t: =SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, criteria_range2, criteria2). The sum range comes first, unlike SUMIF. Example: total quantity for one product and one salesperson. All ranges must be the same size, and * works as a wildcard, as in "A*".
g: Wildcard
* stands for any characters, ? for any single character.

pages.t: =COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, ...) counts the rows where every condition is true, for example open quotes from one salesperson. Criteria can use comparisons like "<5" or ">1". It gives a quick answer without building anything bigger.

quiz.q: In SUMIFS, which argument comes first?
quiz.w: SUMIFS starts with the range to add. SUMIF puts its optional sum range last.

quiz.q: You want how many rows are both Finland and above a limit. Which function?
quiz.w: COUNTIFS counts rows where all listed conditions are met.

quiz.q: What does "A*" match as a criterion?
o: Any text containing exactly one letter
quiz.w: The * wildcard stands for any sequence of characters, so "A*" matches text starting with A.

pages.t: Newer Excel has dynamic array functions. One formula can return a whole list, and the result spills into the cells below. You type it once, in the top cell, and Excel sizes the output itself.
g: Spill
A formula result that flows across several neighbouring cells.

pages.t: =UNIQUE(A2:A500) returns each distinct value once, handy for a clean list of resellers from a long order export. =SORT(array) orders a range, with -1 as the third argument for descending. Combine them: =SORT(UNIQUE(A2:A500)).

=FILTER(array, include, [if_empty]) returns the rows that meet a condition, such as =FILTER(A5:D20,C5:C20=H2,""). The third argument is what shows when nothing matches. These functions exist in Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and 2024.
g: Dynamic array
A formula that returns several values at once, spilling into neighbouring cells.

quiz.q: What do you get from =UNIQUE(A2:A500)?
quiz.w: UNIQUE returns a list of the distinct values.

quiz.q: Why give FILTER a third argument?
o: To choose what shows when nothing matches
quiz.w: The if_empty argument sets the result when no rows pass. Otherwise you get an error.

quiz.q: Which formula gives a sorted list of distinct resellers?
quiz.w: Wrapping UNIQUE in SORT sorts the distinct list.

pages.t: On Windows, Ctrl+Arrow jumps to the edge of the current data region. Ctrl+Home goes to the start of the sheet and Ctrl+End to the last used cell. Ctrl+Page Down moves to the next sheet.
g: Data region
A block of filled cells with no blank rows or columns.

pages.t: Ctrl+Shift+Arrow extends the selection to the last non-blank cell. Ctrl+Space selects the whole column and Shift+Space the whole row. Combine: Ctrl+Home, then Ctrl+Shift+Arrow down, selects a column of data in two moves.
F2 edits the active cell. Ctrl+Z undoes and Ctrl+Y repeats the last action. Make Ctrl+Z a reflex before you panic about a big paste or delete. And Ctrl+; enters the current date.

quiz.q: Which shortcut jumps to the last used cell on a sheet?
quiz.w: Ctrl+End moves to the last used cell. Ctrl+Home goes to the start.

quiz.q: How do you select a whole column quickly on Windows?
quiz.w: Ctrl+Space selects an entire column, Shift+Space an entire row.

quiz.q: What does F2 do?
quiz.w: F2 edits the active cell with the cursor at the end of its content.

quiz.q: What does Ctrl+Arrow do?
o: Jumps to the edge of the data region
quiz.w: It moves to the edge of the current data region.

src.l: Microsoft: Using Flash Fill in Excel

pages.t: Ctrl+D fills the top cell's content down through the selection. Flash Fill (Ctrl+E) spots a pattern: type the first surname by hand next to a full-name column, press Ctrl+E, and Excel completes the rest.
g: Flash Fill
Excel recognises your pattern and fills the rest of the column.

pages.t: On a long price list, the headers scroll away. Use View, Freeze Panes. Excel freezes the rows above and the columns left of the selected cell. Select A2 first to freeze just the top row. Unfreeze Panes reverses it.
g: Freeze panes
Keeps chosen rows and columns visible while you scroll.

pages.t: Ctrl+Alt+V opens Paste Special. Press V to paste only the values, not the formulas. This is how you turn a calculated column into fixed numbers, or share figures without dragging formulas along.
g: Paste Special
Paste menu that lets you choose values, formats or formulas separately.

quiz.q: You want to paste figures without their formulas. What do you use?
quiz.w: Paste Special with Values pastes only the numbers, not the formulas.

quiz.q: Which cell do you select to freeze only the top row?
quiz.w: Freeze Panes freezes the rows above the selected cell, so select A2.

quiz.q: What does Ctrl+E trigger?
quiz.w: Ctrl+E invokes Flash Fill, which fills the current column based on a pattern.

src.l: Microsoft: Top ten ways to clean your data
Microsoft: Apply data validation to cells

pages.t: A list works best with one header row, similar data in each column, no blank rows and all rows visible. An Excel table helps with this. Keep one list per sheet, so filters and formulas always know where the data starts and stops.

Data, Data Validation restricts what can be typed into a cell: whole numbers, dates, or a drop-down list of allowed choices such as country names. That prevents Finland, finland and FI all appearing in one column.
g: Data validation
A rule limiting what a cell accepts, such as a drop-down list.

pages.t: Before analysing an export, keep an untouched backup copy. =TRIM(A2) removes extra spaces, but not the web-style nonbreaking space. Remove Duplicates deletes repeated rows. Name files clearly, for example with a date, so versions never get mixed up.
g: TRIM
Removes extra spaces from text, leaving single spaces between words.

quiz.q: A drop-down list of allowed countries is made with which feature?
quiz.w: Data Validation with the List type creates a drop-down.

quiz.q: Why keep a backup copy before cleaning an export?
o: To be able to return to the original data
quiz.w: Microsoft's cleaning guide recommends keeping a backup of the original.

quiz.q: Which setup works best for a customer list?
o: One header row, no blank rows, one list per sheet
quiz.w: Tabular data with a header row and no blank rows works best with filters and formulas.

pages.t: If numbers sit left-aligned, often with a green triangle, they may be text. Calculations can skip them. Select the cells and use the warning button to Convert to Number. SUM ignores text values, so a total that looks too low is a reason to check.
g: Text-formatted number
A number Excel treats as text, so calculations skip it.

pages.t: For visible cells only, use SUBTOTAL. =SUBTOTAL(109,B2:B10) sums while ignoring manually hidden rows, while 9 includes them. Rows filtered out are always left out of SUBTOTAL.
g: SUBTOTAL
A summing function that can ignore hidden or filtered rows.

pages.t: Formatting to two decimals only shows two, the full number is still stored. =ROUND(A1,2) actually rounds the value. =TODAY() updates every day, so it is wrong for a date you want to keep, like a quote date.

quiz.q: Numbers are left-aligned with a green triangle. What is likely?
quiz.w: Left alignment and the indicator often mean numbers formatted as text.

quiz.q: Which formula sums only visible rows, ignoring manually hidden ones?
quiz.w: Function number 109 ignores manually hidden rows, 9 includes them.

quiz.q: What does formatting a cell to two decimals do?
quiz.w: Formatting changes the look. Use ROUND to change the value itself.

quiz.q: Why is =TODAY() a bad choice for a quote date you want to keep?
quiz.w: TODAY returns the current date and updates daily, so the saved date would drift.

src.l: Microsoft: Get started with Copilot in Excel
Microsoft: Overview of PivotTables and PivotCharts
Microsoft: About Power Query in Excel

pages.t: Click key result cells and read the formula bar. Look for hard-typed numbers inside formulas, error values and totals that look off. Test with a simple case you can calculate by hand. If a sheet feeds a customer decision, ask the author how it works.

PivotTables condense large data sets for interactive analysis. Power Query connects to outside data and reshapes it. Both are worth learning later, and this app does not teach them. Keep records that many people update at once in a shared system, not in one Excel file.
g: PivotTable
An interactive summary table of a large data set.
Power Query
A built-in tool to connect to and reshape data.

pages.t: With a Microsoft 365 subscription that includes Copilot, and your organisation allowing it, Copilot can help with your data. It has edit, plan and chat-only modes. Plan shows steps first, and chat-only changes nothing. Always check its results yourself.
g: Copilot
Microsoft's AI assistant built into Microsoft 365 apps.

quiz.q: What is a good first step when auditing a colleague's sheet?
o: Click result cells and read the formulas
quiz.w: Reading the formula in the formula bar shows how a result was built.

quiz.q: What does Power Query do?
o: Connects to outside data and reshapes it
quiz.w: Power Query imports or connects to data, then transforms it.

quiz.q: Which Copilot mode proposes steps before changing anything?
quiz.w: Plan mode proposes a plan for you to confirm before changes are made.

quiz.q: What is required to use Copilot in Excel?
o: Nothing, it is free in all versions
A Microsoft 365 subscription that includes Copilot, allowed by your organisation
quiz.w: Copilot must be included in your Microsoft 365 subscription and allowed by your organisation.
